criteria.criterion: Run `cargo test -p athena-cli status_and_stop_find_the_drain_by_pid_file`: the fixed test passes, and a new test that makes the stand-in exit before the waiting stop_and_wait call passes deterministically by asserting the old failure outcome NotRunning(Dead(pid)).
criteria.evidence: With the criterion's filter, status_and_stop_find_the_drain_by_pid_file_when_command_lines_contain_drain passed (1 passed). That filter doesn't match the new test, a_stand_in_drain_that_exited_before_the_waiting_stop_reads_as_dead_not_exited, so I ran it by name and it passed. All 24 drain::tests passed. The new test is deterministic: it writes the release file, calls `drain_child.0.wait()` to reap the stand-in, then calls stop_and_wait with a wait and asserts `StopOutcome::NotRunning(NotRunning::Dead(record.pid))`.

criteria.criterion: In the diff, the fixed test's stand-in does not exit on the stop file alone; it also waits for a release file that the test creates after the waiting stop_and_wait call has started, with no reliance on sleeps to win the race.
criteria.evidence: The script is now `while [ ! -e "$1" ] || [ ! -e "$2" ]; do sleep 0.05; done` with $2 as the release file. ReleaseAfterFirstLookup::start_marker reads the real marker first, then writes the release file once, guarded by an AtomicBool swap. In stop_and_wait (drain.rs:3784) the first lookup is the drain_state call inside the waiting call, so the stand-in is alive when it is read and can exit only afterwards. The sleep in the shell loop is only its poll interval. No sleep decides the order.

criteria.criterion: The original test's assertions on the pid file record, drain_status output, Asked outcome, stop file existence, Exited(record) result, and decoy untouched remain with unchanged meaning.
criteria.evidence: drain.rs:5212-5252 keeps every check: drain_state Running(found)==record; status contains the pid, BUILD and 'running' and not the decoy's pid; Asked(record) from the first call, which still uses RealProcs; stop_file exists; Exited(record); settled is NotRunning::Dead; decoy try_wait is None. The only difference is the Procs passed to the waiting call. It delegates to RealProcs, so the lookup results are the same.

The new test, a_stand_in_drain_that_exited_before_the_waiting_stop_reads_as_dead_not_exited, had to be run with its own filter. A name sharing the prefix would let the one command cover both.

findings.summary: The reproduction test reaps the stand-in before the waiting call. If the OS reused that pid in between, the outcome would be Recycled, not Dead.
findings.evidence: `drain_child.0.wait()` frees the pid before stop_and_wait looks it up. Reuse within that short window is very unlikely (estimate, not measured). Leaving the child as an unreaped zombie would read as Dead with no reuse risk, because linux_marker returns None for state Z.

summary: The change fixes the race in the test only and makes it deterministic. The stand-in drain now loops until both the stop file and a release file exist. The waiting stop_and_wait call is handed a `Procs` wrapper, `ReleaseAfterFirstLookup`, which creates the release file right after its first start-marker read. So stop_and_wait always sees the stand-in alive before it starts waiting, and the stand-in can only exit after that. No sleep or thread is needed to win the race. A new test makes the stand-in exit and reaps it before the waiting call, then asserts NotRunning(Dead(pid)), which is the outcome the CI run failed on. Production stop_and_wait is unchanged. The new test's comment gives the reason: a dead pid that was never seen running cannot be told apart from a crashed or stale drain. Every original check is still there with the same meaning: the pid-file record, the drain_status output, the decoy missing from that output, Asked, the stop file existing, Exited(record), the Dead state once settled, and the decoy left running. I ran the fixed test, the new test and all 24 drain unit tests in this snapshot, and all passed. Athena's recorded fmt, clippy and test runs passed. Only drain.rs and CHANGELOG.md changed, and the CHANGELOG entry describes only the test change. There are two minor findings: the new test's name doesn't match the criterion-1 filter, so I ran it by name; and after reaping, its pid could in theory be reused, which would read as Recycled.
